newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia rejects DEA heroin trafficking charge.
newsitem.headline: Colombia rejects DEA heroin trafficking charge.

text.p: Colombian officials have rejected U.S. charges that almost two-thirds of the heroin entering the United States comes from Colombia, a confidential report obtained by Reuters on Wednesday said.
U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration chief Thomas Constantine set up a joint force with Colombian police to stem heroin trafficking during a brief visit to Bogota on Tuesday.
He said Colombia was now supplying 63 percent of the heroin sold on U.S. streets, mainly in East Coast cities.
But the report drawn up by the Drugs Observatory, a drug monitoring unit that works out of President Ernesto Samper's office, refuted that figure.

"If Colombian heroin production is scarcely two percent of the world total, as reflected in United Nations figures, it is not possible that 63 percent of the heroin entering the United States is from Colombia," the report said.
According to Colombian National Police, Colombia produced 6.5 tons of heroin last year, 85 percent of which was smuggled into the United States with the remainder going to Europe.
Colombia is the world's largest producer of cocaine. Its heroin trade only started in this decade.
Constantine said heroin exports began shortly after Colombian growers contracted processing experts from Pakistan or Afghanistan to improve the quality of their product.

"About 63 percent of all heroin we seize in the United States comes from Colombia. That doesn't mean to say 63 percent of all the heroin entering the United States is from Colombia, but it's a pretty good indication," he told reporters in Bogota.

He added that Baltimore, Boston, Orlando and New York were the cities hardest hit by the new demand for heroin, which he said was driven by the "jet set and entertainment elite" who viewed the opiate as a new "wonder drug".
The DEA boss praised the Colombian police for their role in fighting all forms of drug-trafficking. He called them "one of the most professional forces in the hemisphere".
The drug monitoring report, however, rejected the U.S. assessment and said Colombia was well behind the Golden Triangle of southwest Asia as a heroin producer.
"One cannot deny that the production of Colombia heroin has increased this decade but one cannot say that we have become one of the world's biggest producers," the report said.

The United Nations Drug Control Programme has estimated that there were 672,000 acres (280,000 hectares) of opium poppy plantations in the world last year, of which 15,700 acres (6,540 hectares), or 2.3 percent, were in Colombia.
Constantine conceded that the DEA estimates on the size of the Colombian heroin trade could be controversial when viewed alongside U.N. figures.

"Last year people looked at our figures as some kind of insult to Colombia but I think now they recognise these figures are correct. The (Colombian) National Police are an effective law enforcement agency and I trust they will do all they can," he said.
